rationale: Method: each work contributes exactly one passage, so the work rate is count__domains__DISTANCE_TRAVEL / n_passages (0 or 1). I averaged works within each genre-by-period cell (late means year >= 1876), took late minus early within each of the 8 genres, and averaged the 8 genre differences with equal weight. Point estimate: +0.025 passage-rate units. A bootstrap that resamples works within each genre-by-period cell (1000 draws) gives a 95% CI of [0.002, 0.045]. Resampling by author gives [0.000, 0.048]. An OLS with genre, origin and date-confidence controls and author-clustered SEs gives 0.022 with CI [-0.002, 0.045], so that interval includes zero. The sign is positive in every subset I checked: high-confidence dates only 0.015, no low-confidence dates 0.020, UK 0.033, US 0.019, unknown origin 0.028, excluding 'other' and 'collection' 0.020, works from 1850-1900 only 0.014, and alternative cutoffs of 1870 and 1885 give 0.019 and 0.028. Two genres (adventure and sensation_mystery) go down, not up. The weak points are coverage and size. Early cells are small (37-165 works per genre), and romance has 0 of 40 early works with the domain, which inflates its difference. The decade series is noisy: 0.10 in the 1860s, 0.06 in the 1870s, then about 0.09-0.12 afterwards. The effect is small, and its significance depends on the specification and is marginal (the lower bound is near zero). Other possible explanations: changes in genre mix within the 'other' and 'collection' groups, misdated works, a few prolific authors, and labeling drift. The cited passages are only examples of the construct, labeled early and late. They cannot show a trend. Because the evidence for a modest increase is consistent in sign but too weak to call a robust historical shift, I abstain.
